cards.rueckseite: Junction of the **frontal, parietal, temporal bones and greater wing of the sphenoid**. About **two fingerbreadths above the zygomatic arch** and **a thumb's breadth behind the frontal process of the zygomatic bone**.
Junction of the **lambdoid, occipitomastoid and parietomastoid sutures**. Overlies the lower half of the **transverse–sigmoid sinus junction**.

- **Bregma:** coronal + sagittal sutures
- **Lambda:** lambdoid + sagittal sutures
- **Inion:** below the external occipital protuberance, overlies the torcula
- **Opisthion:** posterior midline margin of the foramen magnum

cards.text: Sylvian fissure line: from the {{c1::frontozygomatic point (2.5 cm up the orbital rim)}} to the {{c2::75% point}} of the nasion–inion line. The pterion lies {{c3::3 cm}} behind the frontozygomatic point along this line.

Upper Rolandic point: {{c1::2 cm posterior to the 50% point}} of the nasion–inion line. Lower Rolandic point: where the line to the midzygomatic arch meets the Sylvian line, about {{c2::2.5 cm behind the pterion}}. Motor strip is usually {{c3::4–5.4 cm}} behind the coronal suture.

cards.vorderseite: Approaches to the posterior third ventricle / pineal region
cards.rueckseite:
- Supracerebellar infratentorial
- Occipital (suboccipital) transtentorial
- Interhemispheric transcallosal (splenium)
- Transcortical parietal (seldom used)

cards.vorderseite: Transchoroidal approach to the third ventricle
cards.rueckseite: Via transcallosal/transcortical route into the lateral ventricle, displace the choroid plexus, divide the **tela choroidea** and enter the third ventricle **between the choroid plexus and the fornix** (alternative: interforniceal).

cards.vorderseite: Histological features distinguishing glioma grades II → III → IV
cards.rueckseite:
- **III vs. II:** mitotic activity
- **IV (GBM):** additionally **necrosis** (often pseudopalisading) and/or **microvascular proliferation**
cards.notiz: CNBR p. 597. WHO 2021: IDH-wildtype diffuse astrocytoma with TERT promoter mutation, EGFR amplification or +7/−10 is graded as GBM even without necrosis.

cards.rueckseite:
Maximal safe resection, then
- **RT 60 Gy** in 2 Gy fractions, 5 days/week for 6 weeks
- **Concurrent temozolomide 75 mg/m²** daily
- Then **6 cycles adjuvant temozolomide 150–200 mg/m²**, days 1–5 of 28

- **MGMT promoter methylation**
- **IDH mutation** ("secondary" GBM from lower-grade tumors, younger patients ~45 y, OS 27–31 months)
- Age < 50
- Good KPS, greater extent of resection
cards.notiz: CNBR p. 601. WHO 2021: IDH-mutant tumors are now 'astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, grade 4'; GBM is by definition IDH-wildtype.

cards.rueckseite: WHO grade I, children (median age 13). Posterior fossa, optic pathway/hypothalamus, brainstem. **Cyst with enhancing mural nodule**. Histology: **Rosenthal fibers, eosinophilic granular bodies**. Associated with **NF1** (optic glioma). Cerebellar: resect nodule (cyst wall need not be removed). ~80% 20-year survival.

WHO grade I, in the lateral ventricle wall near the **foramen of Monro**. Occurs in **5–15% of tuberous sclerosis** patients (mean age 13). Symptomatic by obstructing the foramen. No malignant transformation. Treatment: resection (excellent prognosis).

WHO grade II (2016), superficial cortical tumor of children/young adults (peak 10–19 y), presents with **seizures**. **Cyst with enhancing mural nodule**. 15–20% malignant transformation. Often cured by surgery alone (5-y survival 81%).
**IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted**, WHO grade II. Peak 35–44 y. 2/3 present with **seizures**. **Frontal lobe** > 50%. Often **calcified**. Median survival 8–11 years.

cards.vorderseite: Low-grade diffuse astrocytoma: adverse prognostic factors
cards.rueckseite:
- Age > 40
- Tumor > 6 cm
- Crossing the midline
- Focal neurological deficit

Most common **primary spinal cord tumor** (adults: 60% spinal); third most common pediatric CNS tumor. Pediatric intracranial ependymomas typically arise from the **floor of the 4th ventricle** (peak 10–15 y). **Myxopapillary** variant: filum terminale, favorable. Intramedullary lesions often with **syrinx**.
Maximal resection (extent of resection = most important prognostic factor), then fractionated radiation. **Spine MRI + lumbar CSF cytology** to rule out drop metastases; spinal RT if positive.
WHO grade I, usually **incidental in older patients**. Sharply demarcated intraventricular nodule (often 4th ventricle), enhancement uncommon. Rarely needs surgery.

Papilloma WHO I, carcinoma WHO III. Papilloma ~5× more common. > 80% of carcinomas in children < 3 y. Present with **hydrocephalus** (CSF overproduction/obstruction). Both can seed the neuraxis. 5-y survival 80% vs. 40%. Associations: Aicardi (papilloma), **Li–Fraumeni** (carcinoma).

- **Tectal:** hydrocephalus, very benign (80% 5-y PFS) → follow-up, CSF diversion
- **Focal tegmental:** hemiparesis, slow → resection
- **Diffuse intrinsic pontine (DIPG):** multiple cranial nerve palsies, ataxia; median survival **< 1 year**

Dysplastic cerebellar gangliocytoma (WHO I), young adults. Associated with **Cowden syndrome (PTEN)**. MRI: **striated "tiger-stripe"** cerebellar pattern. Presents with raised ICP/hydrocephalus. Resection usually curative.
WHO I, almost all < 2 y (peak 3–6 months). **Very large frontoparietal** cyst with **dural-based enhancing plaque**. Increased head size, bulging fontanelle. Complete resection curative.

WHO I, children/young adults. Chronic **refractory epilepsy** with partial seizures before age 20, no focal deficit. Cortical, pseudocystic ("bubbly"), minimal enhancement, often with adjacent **cortical dysplasia**. Resection: seizure freedom 85% at 5 y.
Mixed ganglion and glial cells, WHO I–II. Young patients (peak 11). **Temporal lobe in 60–70%**, epilepsy. Often **cyst with mural nodule**, may calcify. Resection: seizure freedom ~75–80%.

WHO II, 20–40 y. **Lateral ventricle near the foramen of Monro**, attached to the septum. Lobulated, **calcified in ~50%**, "bubbly". Presents with hydrocephalus. Histologic DDx: oligodendroglioma. Resection usually curative.

Non-neoplastic malformation of the tuber cinereum/hypothalamus. Presents with **gelastic (laughing) seizures** and **precocious puberty**. Intrahypothalamic (90%) vs. parahypothalamic (pedunculated). Surgery/disconnection to stop seizures.

cards.notiz: CNBR Table 6.13. Treatment: α/β-blockade, preoperative embolization, resection; RT if inoperable.

cards.rueckseite: **Hydrocephalus** (aqueduct compression) and **Parinaud syndrome** (upgaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus, light-near dissociation).

**Pineocytoma:** slow growing, peak 10–20 y, 5-y survival ~90%, resection.
**Pineoblastoma:** embryonal (PNET-like), young children (peak 3 y), **CSF seeding in ~50%**, median survival 2 y; resection + craniospinal RT (if > 3 y) + chemotherapy.

WHO IV embryonal tumor, most common malignant pediatric brain tumor (~40% of pediatric posterior fossa tumors), M:F 3:1, most diagnosed by age 5. Midline **4th ventricle/vermis**, highly cellular → **restricted diffusion**. CSF metastases at presentation in ~30%. Isochromosome/loss of **17p** in 40–50%.

**Standard:** age ≥ 3 y, no metastases, no gross residual after resection → 5-y survival very high.
**High risk:** age < 3 y, metastases, or residual tumor → 5-y survival ~20% (book).
Treatment: resection, chemotherapy, **craniospinal RT if > 3 y**.
cards.notiz: CNBR p. 607. Modern risk stratification also uses molecular groups (WNT, SHH, group 3, group 4).

cards.rueckseite: Almost always **< 3 years**, highly malignant, often posterior fossa (DDx medulloblastoma). Loss of **INI1 (SMARCB1)**. CSF seeding ~20%. Median survival ~17 months. RT usually not possible because of age.

- **Observation** (< 3 cm): MRI/audiology every 6 months
- **Radiosurgery** for growing tumors < 3 cm: ~90% control, rare facial palsy, 50–90% hearing preservation
- **Surgery** for all > 3 cm: ~80% normal/near-normal facial nerve
- Approaches: **translabyrinthine** (sacrifices hearing, good CN VII), **retrosigmoid/suboccipital** (hearing preservation), middle fossa

cards.text: Neurofibromas (especially plexiform, in {{c1::NF1, chromosome 17}}) degenerate into {{c2::malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor}} in {{c3::2–12%}}.

cards.rueckseite:
- **Grade I (75–80%):** meningothelial, fibrous, transitional, psammomatous, angiomatous, microcystic, secretory, lymphoplasmacyte-rich, metaplastic
- **Grade II (15–25%):** atypical, **clear cell**, **chordoid**, brain-invasive
- **Grade III (1–2%):** anaplastic, **rhabdoid**, **papillary**

cards.text: Meningioma risk factors: prior {{c1::radiation}}, {{c2::NF2}}; F:M about {{c3::2:1}}; multiple in up to 8%.

zeilen: Complete, including dural attachment and abnormal bone

cards.rueckseite: WHO I, 1–2% of intracranial tumors, most common primary intra-axial **posterior fossa tumor in adults**. **25–40% with von Hippel–Lindau**. **Cyst with enhancing mural nodule**, can cause **polycythemia** (EPO). Resection of the nodule ± preoperative embolization.

Up to 10% of primary brain tumors, increased in AIDS. Periventricular, homogeneously enhancing, restricted diffusion. **Stereotactic biopsy** (no resection), then **high-dose methotrexate**-based chemotherapy ± RT. **Avoid steroids before biopsy** (dramatic transient response can make diagnosis impossible).
Often mimics a meningioma. High risk of **multiple myeloma** within 10 years → rule out myeloma (urine protein/Bence-Jones, serum protein electrophoresis). Resection followed by radiation.

50% of pineal region tumors, more common in Japan, 90% < 20 y. **Pineal: M ≫ F** (Parinaud, hydrocephalus); **suprasellar: more often F** (**diabetes insipidus**, visual loss, hypopituitarism). Very radio- and chemosensitive, 5-y survival > 90%. Biopsy + RT/chemo; ETV can allow biopsy.

cards.notiz: Standard marker pattern (CNBR refers to Ch. 3 section IX).

cards.text: Prolactin levels: < 25 ng/mL {{c1::normal}}; 25–150 ng/mL {{c2::possible stalk effect}}; > 150 ng/mL {{c3::almost diagnostic of prolactinoma}}.

cards.titel: Pituitary adenomas: presentation and first-line treatment

cards.rueckseite: Immediate **high-dose corticosteroids** (adrenal insufficiency) ± **emergent transsphenoidal decompression** (visual loss, reduced consciousness).

2–5% of intracranial tumors, bimodal (children 5–10 y, adults). Benign but relentless; cystic ("machinery oil"), **calcified** (adamantinomatous). Preop: treat **adrenal insufficiency** (hydrocortisone). Postop: **diabetes insipidus**, hypothalamic injury. Gross total resection if safe, RT after subtotal resection.

cards.notiz: CNBR Table 6.16. Metastases = most common brain tumor (multiple in 50–70%) and most common adult posterior fossa tumor.

cards.rueckseite:
- **Dexamethasone:** 4–8 mg/d for mild symptoms, 16 mg/d for significant mass effect
- **No prophylactic AEDs** in seizure-free patients
- **Surgery** for symptomatic accessible lesions, then SRS to the cavity
- **SRS alone** for 1–4 metastases with good performance status
- WBRT mainly palliative (many metastases, SCLC)

zeilen: KPS ≥ 70, age < 65, controlled primary, no extracranial mets

cards.rueckseite: Both ~1% of brain tumors, slow linear growth. **Epidermoid:** lateral (CPA), **bright on DWI**, **aseptic (Mollaret) meningitis**. **Dermoid:** midline, fat (T1 bright), **septic meningitis** (dermal sinus). Excision; perioperative steroids reduce chemical meningitis.

< 1% of tumors, age 20–50, at the **foramen of Monro** (anterior 3rd ventricle). Can cause acute obstructive hydrocephalus and **sudden death**. Excision endoscopically or open (transcallosal/transcortical).

From notochord remnants; 35% clival, 50% sacral; peak 50–60 y. **Abducens (VI) palsy** typical. T2 very bright, enhancing, midline osteolytic. Recurrence ~85% after surgery. **Wide en bloc resection + postop radiation (proton beam)**.
